newsitem.title: USA: Texas wheat harvest begins, rust cuts yields.
newsitem.headline: Texas wheat harvest begins, rust cuts yields.

text.p: The hard red winter wheat harvest was slowly advancing in southern Texas, but should gain momentum the next 10 days with crop sources expecting high proteins, but average yields and test weights.
Weeds and rust were widespread, with rust cutting 10 bushels per acre off yields in some areas, sources said.
Harvest in Frio County, southwest of San Antonio, produced early yields of 15 to 25 bushels an acre, up from 10 bushels a year ago, said Mac Wilmeth, manager of Dilley Feed and Grain.
"The quality seems real good," said Wilmeth. However, because of twice the normal April rainfall, weed populations were high which slowed harvesting, he said.
The fungus rust was widespread in south Texas and crop sources estimated it could cut 10 bushels an acre off yields.
"If we didn't have rust we could have had yields up to 40 bushels," said Charles Stickler, a south Texas extension agronomist, who was forecasting a 30-bushel average.
Wheat delivered Tuesday to Corpus Christi's Interstate Grain Corp elevator had 13 to 14 percent protein and test weights were varied.
"I would say the yields should be excellent this year because we've had a lot of rain," said Lloyd Schultz, Interstate's vice president.
As of Sunday, the Texas Agricultural Statistics Service rated the state's winter wheat 27 percent good to excellent, 41 percent fair, 21 poor and 11 percent very poor.

Texas wheat damaged by the mid-April freeze was further north in the Panhandle and along the Red River bordering Oklahoma. The Statistics Service said freeze damage there ranged from slight to severe but growth had resumed in these damaged fields.
The April freeze also hit Kansas and Oklahoma wheat and in Kansas the crop improved slightly this past week, while damage was still being assessed in Oklahoma.
Leaf rust and wheat streak mosaic was present in Kansas wheat as well as alfalfa weevil and aphids. Wheat was headed in southeast Kansas.

Participants of this week's Wheat Quality Council tour through Kansas found healthy wheat in north central and east central Kansas that could match or exceed last year's yields. The tour has not yet viewed wheat in southwest Kansas that was hit by the freeze.
Kansas wheat as of Sunday was rated eight percent excellent, 47 good, 34 fair, nine poor and two very poor versus the previous week of three excellent, 52 good, 31 fair, 11 poor and three very poor.

"The extent of the freeze damage from three weeks ago is questionable," the latest Oklahoma Agricultural Statistics Service report said. "As a general rule, farmers have still kept grain production in their sights."
Oklahoma wheat as of Sunday was rated 33 percent good to excellent, 35 fair, 18 poor and four very poor.
